segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There are certain things you should really only say to your best friend. This is probably one of them.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Do you ever just shut up and just listen to somebody?

segments.speaker: Scott
segments.text: Go right ahead.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: That's what-- spill it out there, brother.

segments.speaker: Scott
segments.text: I already did.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Tom and Scott are in an all-night diner around midnight. Scott is disheveled and tired. He's been working all night as a bartender at a Chinese restaurant, serving lots of free drinks on the sly to Tom. And Tom, in response, seems astonishingly ungrateful. Here is the kind of sass that Tom keeps throwing Scott's way.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: You're the-- you're the one who needed the food and the beers and all that stuff like that to calm down after your traumatic night stealing from your employer.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Just at that moment, a man in a Hawaiian print shirt and khaki pants walks by their table. He hears the word "employer," mistakes it for the word "lawyer," and then turns to Tom.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Are you a lawyer?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: No. Do you want to be?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Who brought up a lawyer to start with? You just came-- walked in--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: You did.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: No, I didn't. Not at all.

segments.speaker: Scott
segments.text: He didn't say lawyer.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: You thought that you heard something and then you let your mind take over and then it got you in-- it put you in--

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Well, I am a lawyer, so that's probably why I might have thought that. But you know what? I'm trained in the art of listening, and I could've sworn you said you wanted to be a lawyer.

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Well, I definitely wouldn't hire you because you heard completely wrong.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Tom
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's some conversations that you overhear and it's hard not to want to keep listening or to butt in, even though everybody knows that it is not the right thing to do. One Sunday morning a while back, I was sitting in one of the booths in this very diner, the Golden Apple, in Chicago on Lincoln Avenue, and I looked around the restaurant. The table next to me, a family was taking their teenage daughter out to an awkward last breakfast before she shipped out with the military. There were dressed-up people who'd come in from the church across the street, and young couples who'd stumbled in with the paper and were working on the crossword together. And I thought, if only somebody could interview every person at every table in this restaurant. That would be amazing. You'd get such a wide variety of different kinds of stories from different kinds of people. So we decided to try it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One Friday night, a big group of us took shifts starting at 5:00 AM and going to 5:00 AM the next morning. During quiet hours, it was just one of us on duty, recording and interviewing people. During the busiest hours, which means late night, three or four of us worked the tables. We first broadcast today's program all the way back in 2000, and we'll be running it again today. From WBEZ Chicago, today's show, "24 Hours at the Golden Apple." It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay tuned.

segments.speaker: Pete
segments.text: It's 5 o'clock in the morning. My name is Pete. I work from 10:00 PM to 5:00 AM, and now we're going to have the taxi drivers and the cops, you know, come for a cup of coffee until 6 o'clock, the morning crowd is going to be in.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Pete's one of the three owners of this restaurant, along with Nick and Tom. All three are Greek, and one of them is always there 24 hours a day. The restaurant sits at one of those intersections where three streets come together, not two, so every one of the corners in the intersection is wedge-shaped, which means that the restaurant itself is wedge-shaped, with booths along the windows on two sides of the wedge.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a counter with stools and a larger room with tables in the back. There are those oversized, laminated menus that go on for pages-- pages-- with pictures of the food. By the door is one of those revolving dessert cases, an octagon made of glass. Three shelves of cream pies and melon slices and cakes. Lately, it's been nothing but trouble. Here's Nick, another one of the owners.

segments.speaker: Nick
segments.text: It's supposed to be turning. It's not turning because the motor broke. Jimmy's supposed to come out like three days ago. He's still coming. Now, if you can figure this one out, the-- the pie case is not turning. And believe it or not, it's not selling as good. That's-- that's a truth.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dessert sales are down, he says, by half, ever since it broke. People just like desserts more when they're in motion.

segments.speaker: Nick
segments.text: It catches the eye. You know, when it's turning, it catches the eye and it sells.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Over the course of 24 hours, the staff of the Golden Apple changes, the regulars who come in change, and the atmosphere changes, from quiet in the early morning to crazy hectic late at night when the bars in the neighborhood let out. Nancy Updike took the first shift of our 24-hour surveillance, mic in hand, from 5:00 AM till 10:00 AM.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This is Eddie. He comes to the Golden Apple a few times a week in the mornings and plays the harmonica in the middle of the restaurant for a few minutes. He's in a pale blue shirt and hopping lightly from foot to foot.

segments.speaker: Eddie
segments.text: I might fall down.

segments.speaker: Eddie
segments.text: [HARMONICA]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Eddie heads to the back of the restaurant to play there. No one is complaining. No one is rolling their eyes. In fact, a few people are smiling and saying hi. Eddie is not an outsider here. He's a regular.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Early morning at the Golden Apple is like that, a profoundly democratic place. Early morning welcomes the night shift workers, the unemployed, the retired, the confused, the disappointed, the slightly off. The people who work for themselves and the people who don't work at all anymore, but crave a little morning routine.

segments.speaker: Joe Molica
segments.text: Every morning, I'm here between 4:30 and 5:00. I love the Golden Apple. They're wonderful people. They got good food. And that's it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This is how Joe Molica ends every sentence.

segments.speaker: Joe Molica
segments.text: And that's it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Or sometimes--

segments.speaker: Joe Molica
segments.text: And that's all I could tell you, honey.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Joe's not used to talking about himself. His story comes out bit by bit. Our entire conversation takes place in a different era. He's completely unselfconscious about calling me honey. He bangs on his coffee cup with his spoon to get the waitresses attention for a refill. Please don't try this at home, but he gets away with it.

segments.speaker: Joe Molica
segments.text: I do construction, remodeling, rehab. And that's what I do. I retired. I'm 78 years old. And I gave the business to my two sons and that's it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How did you start that business?

segments.speaker: Joe Molica
segments.text: Through my dad. My dad done the same thing. When I was, I don't know, maybe 10, 11 years old, I started working for him. He was paying me a dime an hour and that was it. Clean up, sweep up the floors that he's working on. What else you want to know, honey?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: At 5:30 in the morning, almost everyone is sitting alone, by choice, it seems. Joe's friend Bob is sitting in his own booth behind Joe. No one's talking much, but it's a comfortable silence. When you're up this early, it's hard not to feel some sense of community with everyone else who's awake. But you don't necessarily want to talk to them.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: As it gets lighter and lighter outside, more people trickle in. A guy with thick, dark blond hair and a face that looks like it could use another six hours' sleep sits down at the counter. His name is Scott Johnson, and he says he usually comes in around 3:30 AM, but today's different.

segments.speaker: Scott Johnson
segments.text: It's about 20 after 7:00.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How did you start coming to the Golden Apple?

segments.speaker: Scott Johnson
segments.text: I own a bar right down the street. It's called Wits. And I own another one on Clark and Oakdale called Jake's.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How did you get into the bar business?

segments.speaker: Scott Johnson
segments.text: Oh, boy. Well, about eight years ago, I turned 30, quit my career, got a divorce, and bought a bar in the same month.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Oh, my god.

segments.speaker: Scott Johnson
segments.text: Took the Etch-a-Sketch and shook it. Just turned it upside down and shook it real hard and changed my life forever.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: It's completely light outside now. Commuter traffic is picking up. The Golden Apple isn't crowded, but all the front booths are taken, and most of the counter. Nick keeps getting deliveries-- orange juice, potatoes-- and his butcher comes by, John Zervas. John is a big man in that way that's the norm in Chicago. Not fat, just big.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: John has been eating at the Golden Apple and supplying its meats for 10 years. When he was eight years old, he became famous for being the youngest butcher in Illinois.

segments.speaker: John Zervas
segments.text: Back in 1979, I was interviewed by Fahey Flynn. I don't know if you remember. Back in 1979, Fahey Flynn was a well-known newsman right here at Channel 7 news before he died in '81. I was the youngest butcher in Illinois in 1979.

segments.speaker: John Zervas
segments.text: And yeah, I've met Governor Thompson down Randolph Street. My father was in a retail business still out on Randolph Street. And that's how I started learning how to cut. So I've been doing this for-- I'm 33 now and since I was, like, eight years old.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You were a butcher when you were eight?

segments.speaker: John Zervas
segments.text: Well, yeah, I'd been involved, you know, cleaning tables. And about 12 years old, I started cutting meat on a band saw.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Wow. Do you remember the first piece of meat you cut?

segments.speaker: John Zervas
segments.text: Pork chops. Piece of pork loin and I sliced it. I remember very well, like it was yesterday. Real slow on a band saw. Pork chops. Pork loins like 18 pounds. First thing I did is cut it down the middle and start from the middle. The trick is, at the end, not to cut your hands when it comes really small. You got to use a special kind of thing that's underneath the band saw, not to put your hand in it because the band saw doesn't have any friends. I mean, if it's going to grab your hand, it's going to cut it.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The front of the Golden Apple is the smoking section. Sitting there is a grayish woman with a fleshy face and wavy hair in one of the small, two-person booths. Her name is Alice Deluca.

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: I work at a purification center. It's sauna, running, vitamins and minerals. It's a program to rid your body of toxins and radiation.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Wow. Have you done the program yourself?

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: Yes, I have.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Now, to the naked eye, it looks like you're smoking and drinking coffee.

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And about to have some sausage. So how does that square with the whole toxins thing?

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: Well, I'm trying to wake up.

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You need some toxins to wake up?

segments.speaker: Alice Deluca
segments.text: I guess so.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: The restaurant never gets crowded this morning. Turnover is slow. People linger over their coffee or their conversation. It's a weekday, so there's no impatient brunch crowd waiting for tables to open up. And if you don't have an office you need to get to, why rush? Donna, the waitress, is finishing up the night shift and getting ready to go home. She's been on since 11:00 PM, but you would never know it to look at her. She's six feet tall and looks like Catherine Deneuve. She's one of the most beautiful people I've ever seen in person.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How long have you been working here?

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Oh, 26 years.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Wow. How old were you when you started?

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Well, you think I'm going to tell you that? [LAUGHS] Are you kidding? My kids don't even know how old I am.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Donna says she's actually not a night person, but she's worked the night shift the entire time, all 26 years. She came to Chicago from Oklahoma City in her early 20s with three kids.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: I was divorced when I came here, and I had married so young, had my children young. No education. And I had a little baby. That's why I started working nights. But this is a great job for that. I mean, working nights, that way you're with them during the day. You don't sleep much, but-- when they're asleep and you're working. And I'm still working the night shift. I don't know why, but I still am.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Every Christmas Eve, Donna brings in a big tray of homemade cookies for the homeless guys and the old men and the taxi drivers-- anyone who shows up that night. Every once in a while, on her afternoon off, she'll go see a play starring one of the actors who come in every night after their own shifts waiting tables. Her customers give her tapes of the bands they're in, bring in their artwork for her see, tell her about their successes and failures. These are people she's known for years.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: It's like home here to me. And when I think about going on a day job, I just can't. It's almost like it'd be another div-- you know, a separation because it's like home when you've been here this long.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Donna runs her shift at the Golden Apple with a lot of compassion and generosity. But like any good waitress, she's also ruthlessly practical. She can be direct when she needs to. Early morning is no time to stand on ceremony.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Honey, I got to get finished with the rest of my work.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: All right. Can I-- are you doing anything to set up or clean up?

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: I got to check and see what I've got to do.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Can I just follow you around and you tell me what you're doing? I'll just like--

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: Well, I don't even know if I have anything more to do. I just didn't want to talk anymore.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Oh, OK.

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: I didn't want to be rude, but--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: No, no, no. You're [INAUDIBLE].

segments.speaker: Donna
segments.text: I just told her I'm tired of talking. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: In the middle of the day, a muted light streams through the windows through a pale haze of cigarette smoke. At certain hours, it feels like everybody is smoking at the Golden Apple. Three industrial smoke-eaters, a non-stop. At lunch, some customers come in, eat quickly, and head back to work after just a half hour, but they're in the minority. Probably 3/4 of the customers are regulars. Many of them stay for hours. Nick, the owner, says some come two or three times a day.

segments.speaker: Nick
segments.text: I mean, they go home and sleep, of course, but this is their base. We got Charlie right now, and there are some that comes twice, three times a day. Floyd, which is right next to him. Mitch. Mitch with his son on the counter. He's a counter man. Mr. Harland there with Steven. They come twice a day. Russ comes about three, four times a day. Al, two, three times a day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At the counter, a man who looks a little bit like the actor Harry Dean Stanton, scruffy and lean, is here for the second time in 24 hours. He gives me what he says is his nickname, Robert. He says he usually just comes for coffee. Can't afford much else.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So why do you come here?

segments.speaker: Robert
segments.text: Just something to do. Coffee. I come over here because I'm single, no wife, no girlfriend. No kids either.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Robert is one of three different men who tell me that they come here in the afternoon to drink coffee and talk to the waitresses. All three actually seem a little shy and intimidated by the waitresses. Robert is so bashful, he has a hard time saying much of anything to them.

segments.speaker: Robert
segments.text: I've never said more than hello, you know, or goodbye. That's all I ever said. I don't know what to do with a pretty girl, what to say. I don't know what to say.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: At a table in the back, Manuel Hernandez is here for the second time today. He's a retired carpenter. Came to Chicago from Mexico in 1965 as one of the workers who built the Sears Tower downtown, one of the tallest buildings in the world. He quit, he says, when they got to the 105th floor.

segments.speaker: Manuel Hernandez
segments.text: It was too windy up there. After two guys, they-- they fall down, and then I quit because I don't want to be the next.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As the afternoon passes, he calls over one of the waitresses, Sherry, and asks her for help reading a document that he got in the mail from an insurance company. He's worried it's some kind of scam. She reads it, tells him no. They've sent him a check. It's real. Sherry says this kind of thing happens all the time. Some of these guys, who else do they have to turn to?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Out on the sidewalk when the weather's good, the restaurant sets up tables. At one, Allison Musgrave and her two kids are eating. Ian is four, Madeline is two. Both are wearing their bicycle helmets at the table and eating the Mickey Mouse pancakes. Three pancakes arranged in violation of US copyright law. Two ears and a head, maraschino cherries, canned pineapple, and whipped cream as the eyes and mouth. Cover it with maple syrup and you have a sugar concoction so powerful that four-year-old Ian literally cannot sit in his chair.

segments.speaker: Allison Musgrave
segments.text: Ian, Ian. Around here, please. Thank you.

segments.speaker: Allison Musgrave
segments.text: [IAN MUTTERING BABY TALK]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't live far from here and I do not think there is a four year old in a 10-block radius who does not know the Mickey Mouse pancakes.

segments.speaker: Allison Musgrave
segments.text: Turn around now, Ian. Turn around, please.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The restaurant has toys for kids in a corner inside. One couple named Mike and Liz tell us that they come here so often with their four and seven year old and feel so at home here that they've instructed their kids that if they're ever lost, they're supposed to find a policeman and tell them not to bring them home. Bring them to the Golden Apple.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As evening falls, it takes a while for the dinner crowd to show up in any kind of force. It's a slow day, everybody says. It is Friday, and couples start to arrive. Some on dates, some just friends. Some in that vague territory in between. The topics of conversation in the room start to make an orbital shift toward couples sorts of topics. One of our producers, Susan Burton, notices one couple in particular.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: A man and a woman in their 30s sit down in a booth by a window. The man's long hair is tied back with a bandanna.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: I'm Daniel Romero. Silvia and I just got through playing a few sets of tennis in Grant Park, and stopped at Healing Earth for a little incense and some good karma. And we decided to stop and grab a bite.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: You know, Sylvia and I have this kind of weird history. She actually dumped me not too long ago. And-- that's right.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: That's a long time ago, Romero.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Well, not that long ago. So she's-- she's now happily in a relationship, and I was telling her as we were driving here about how lonely I am.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: Actually, it's been three years since Daniel and Sylvia broke up. They met when they worked together at the same nonprofit organization.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Well, you're ready to settle down now.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: I am.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Well, I'm proud of you. I'm proud of you. I actually-- when you first told me that, I actually wasn't sure.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: Right. But you will not be coming to the wedding. You already told me that.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: I did-- I did-- I did tell you that. I won't be participating there. You'll have my best wishes.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: Why? We're friends. I still love you and care about you. Why can't you be there?

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Well-- [LAUGHS] well, why can't-- it would just be weird. I mean, you and I have a pretty significant history together. But I would-- I would still be happy for you and you'd have my best wishes, and I'll still buy you a toaster.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: A toaster? OK. See, I think that that's unusual. I think-- I would be very happy for you. Would I have some feelings there? Yeah, maybe there would be a little twinge, thinking why-- why wasn't it me?

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: That's actually a Sex in the City topic a lot.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: In case you've missed it, Sex and the City is a TV show on HBO. Each episode circles around some central question, like, can you be friends with your ex? If Daniel and Sylvia and I were suddenly cast in our own episode of the show, this would be the moment where I would light a cigarette and flip open my PowerBook and ponder what I'd seen.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: Daniel and Sylvia began by talking about Sylvia's new boyfriend, but wound up discussing each other. And I started to wonder, when you talk about your ex's new relationships, are you really just talking about the two of you?

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: I didn't tell you this. You asked me how my love life was a little bit earlier. I did meet somebody about a week ago. Her name is Amy and she works at-- where does she work at? She works at Supercuts. And she was with her-- her boyfriend, actually.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: And she was hitting on you?

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: And she was hitting on me. She said to me, I want to go out with you. And I said, fine, let's go out. She says, well, you have to wait a month because I'm still going out with this idiot over here. I mean, and she's talking about, you know-- so nothing happened though. But nothing happened.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: But you would go out with a woman who would degrade her boyfriend that way? Who would treat the guy that she's supposedly dating that way?

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Yeah, but I'm not going to marry-- I'm not going to marry this girl, you know? I mean-- you know, I mean, I wasn't interested in a lifetime commitment at that moment. I mean, I was much more looking for the immediate gratification.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: That's what you're always looking for.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: That's not entirely true. That's not entirely true.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: Each time Daniel brings up someone he's interested in, Sylvia gets exasperated with him for refusing to make a commitment. It happens when he mentions the woman he saw in a lounge chair by a pool in Las Vegas, and the girl he's taken on a dozen dates, but is pretty sure he wants to break up with. It turns out that this is a conversation they've had before, at the end of their own relationship.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: I was ready for the next step and he was ready to back out. Any time I pressed forward, he went backwards a couple steps.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: You're right. You and I were in a place where you were frustrated because I couldn't move forward. I was frustrated because you were pressing so hard. And right--

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: And then you met the next girl and moved in with her after three weeks. I think it's a hard topic for us both.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Absolutely, absolutely. Yeah, it's just-- you know, the thought of-- you know, it's like--

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: He trails off, staring out the window.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: I don't know, it's kind of hard to-- it's kind of hard to--

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: It is kind of hard to talk when two babes go by.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: Outside on the sidewalk, two girls with blond hair and short skirts approach. They catch Daniel's eye. He mumbles. As the girls stride by the window, he turns his head and follows them from one end of the glass to the other. The gesture seems to happen in slow motion.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: He does that all the time.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Yeah, but I-- I'm not-- but--

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: I know, I know. I'm not saying that.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Yeah, I understand.

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: I'm just saying that when we were together and you did that, that really hurts.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Even if-- even though it's just looking?

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: It says you're not interested in what's going on right here, and that's exactly--

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: No, see, that's--

segments.speaker: Sylvia
segments.text: --you did by doing that. You couldn't even formulate the sentence because your eyeballs were glued to that window.

segments.speaker: Daniel Romero
segments.text: Look, this-- this is another-- this has-- this has been another topic on Sex and the City.

segments.speaker: Susan Burton
segments.text: Just for the record, what actually happened in that episode, the woman got so mad at her boyfriend that she punched him in the face. And then she realized she couldn't change him.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Over by the restaurant's front windows, which look out on St. Alphonsus Catholic church, a huge building, sits Kay Frank, known to her friends as Katie Keane, 75 years old, dressed in a nice outfit and matching scarf. She's here because one of her longtime neighbors, another Golden Apple customer, is laid out dead in the funeral home right across the street. She'll eat and pay her respects. She tells me that she's lived her whole life within walking distance of this very spot.

segments.text: Yeah. I was born and raised on Lakewood 75 years ago. Went to St. Alphonsus School, so this is my neighborhood for a long time.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass

segments.speaker: Kay Frank

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Back then, for instance, a pharmacy was on this spot. Kay and her friends would come here after 11 o'clock mass.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: I'm talking about first year, second year high school, when you didn't go to the kiddie mass anymore at 9 o'clock in the morning. This was like a hangout here after mass. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She points at a section of booths. For years, this neighborhood was all about which parish you belonged to. St. Alphonsus for the Germans, St. Andrews for the Irish and Italian, St. Josaphat for the Polish. Till finally, in the 1960s, that ended. Kay's five sisters and her parents all moved away from the neighborhood.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: I'm the only one that stayed in the neighborhood because we couldn't afford to move out of here. We bought our house in the mid-'60s, '64. And everybody thought the neighborhood was going to change. So of course, they're moving to the suburbs or farther north or farther west.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Change? You mean people thought it wasn't going to be white anymore?

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: They thought-- yes. They thought it was going to go down. That's why people were scared and moved out. So we couldn't afford to move, so we bought a house there for $27,000. I've had offers of $500,000, $550,000 for my house.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Meanwhile, one of her sisters who moved away to avoid the blight of this area, who moved to an area too expensive for Kay or her husband to afford, just sold her house for only $200,000. Gentrification, which spread through this neighborhood in the last 15 years, hasn't made it out to where her sisters live. But around here, on Southport and on Clark and all over, there are little boutiques and several Starbucks, and expensive restaurants with fake European names.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: The neighborhood has changed a lot, you know? A whole lot. Some for the better, some for the worse. Close by, we have our gay people, which we never had as a kid. They were around, maybe, but we didn't know who they were. Today, you know who they are.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: My husband, coming from the old school-- we have the nicest neighbors we've ever had, two gay men. They can't do enough for you. They cut your grass for you. They water-- now that I'm older. And when they moved in, my husband, coming from way back, oh, my god, you know, he didn't want really too much to do with them.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: Within a year, I'd say, we saw that they were nice people, very clean. And when we had our 50th wedding anniversary party, had some [NON-ENGLISH] here, it was our neighbors that went to the hall without any-- they wouldn't take a penny. They decorated that place like you wouldn't believe. Now, how many neighbors would do that for you, you know?

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: So gay or not gay, they're really nice people. So I think that the gays can be credited for being such a nice people. They swayed a lot of the old-time people into different thinking. There's still a lot of racial stuff. Maybe if you had a black neighbor here, or one of the people would rent to a black person, I think they'd be frowned upon a little bit. But if you rent to a gay person today, it's OK.

segments.speaker: Kay Frank
segments.text: A lot of things that we think should be this way and that way as you grow up, it's really not that way, shouldn't be that way. So I don't feel that we should really judge them, you know? Let the Lord judge them.

segments.speaker: Norman Knudsen
segments.text: One thing that happens is, when you get a regular partner-- and even somebody you can work for the first night. You learn their first name, not just their last. And then, where did you work before, are you married? He collects hockey cards. I collect monster memorabilia. Models. I do model collecting. I collect a couple of guitars. I play the guitar. And then you create a bond. You even tell some intimate secrets, you know, things that even the wives don't know about. But you're creating a bond, and people don't realize that. 90% of the job is you and your partner in the car. It can be a long night or it can be a lot of fun.
